cmimc-2024-tcs-02a.title: Counting bound and Hall's theorem
cmimc-2024-tcs-02a.body:
**Lower bound.** Different $n$-card hands $S\ne S'$ must lead Alice to show Bob different ordered $(n-1)$-tuples (if both showed the same tuple $T$, Bob could name only one hidden card, but $S=T\cup\{h\}$ and $S'=T\cup\{h'\}$ have $h\ne h'$). So we need at least as many ordered $(n-1)$-tuples as hands: $\binom{52}{n}\le52\cdot51\cdots(54-n)$. For $n=4$: $\binom{52}4=270725>52\cdot51\cdot50=132600$, so $n=4$ is impossible; for $n\le3$ the inequality fails as well ($\binom{52}{3}=22100>52\cdot51=2652$, $\binom{52}2=1326>52$, and for $n=1$ Bob sees nothing).

**Construction for $n=5$.** Build a bipartite graph: left vertices are the $\binom{52}5$ hands; right vertices are ordered $4$-tuples of distinct cards. Join a hand $S$ to a tuple $T$ when the cards of $T$ are $S$ minus one card. Each hand has $5\cdot4!=120$ neighbours, and each tuple has $52-4=48$ neighbours. For any set $X$ of hands, the number of edges leaving $X$ is $120|X|$, and these edges land on $N(X)$ whose vertices each receive at most $48$ edges, so $|N(X)|\ge120|X|/48\ge|X|$. By Hall's theorem there is a matching that assigns to every hand a distinct tuple. Alice shows Bob the tuple matched to her hand; Bob finds the matched hand and names the card of that hand that is missing from the tuple. So $n=5$ works.

The lowest $n$ is $5$.

**Answer: $5$**
